title: Programming Languages and Frameworks
answer: The languages AI is written in and the frameworks built on top of them, tracked by adoption, releases, licence, and integrations.

reading.body:
The tracked stack splits into 7 programming languages, 17 AI frameworks, and 12 inference engines, with frameworks the most crowded layer by count.

The pattern is a three-tier stack. Languages sit at the bottom with the fewest entries, because a language either works for AI or it does not. Frameworks sit in the middle and multiply, because each one is a bet on how models should be wired into applications. Inference engines sit above the hardware and below the frameworks, and their count reflects how many ways there are to serve a model.

For AI specifically, the framework layer is where lock-in forms. A team that builds on one of 17 frameworks has chosen an abstraction over model calls, and that choice outlives any single model. The inference layer matters for a different reason: it is the part of the stack that touches GPUs directly, so its diversity is a measure of how many separate paths exist from a model to the silicon.

The data does not say which of these are growing, which are declining, or how much any of them is used. It gives names and counts, not adoption. It also does not connect any of these layers to power or buildings, and nothing here supports a claim about compute demand.
